opus-5.5.text:
Agentic applications are where speed really compounds. When you have a single chatbot response, waiting a few seconds is tolerable. But an agent might make dozens or even hundreds of model calls to finish one task: planning, calling a tool, reading the result, reflecting, retrying. Every one of those calls sits on the critical path, so latency adds up quickly. Because Mercury is a diffusion model, it generates many tokens in parallel and refines them, rather than producing them one at a time left to right. That gives us much higher throughput and lower latency, and in an agent loop that difference gets multiplied across every step.

Coding agents are probably the clearest example. Developers want to stay in flow, and things like autocomplete, next-edit suggestions, and quick refactors need to come back almost instantly. Then there are longer-horizon coding agents that edit files, run tests, look at failures, and iterate. Being several times faster there means you can either finish sooner or afford more iterations in the same time budget, and more iterations often means better final quality.

Speed also makes test-time compute more practical. If generation is cheap and fast, you can sample multiple candidate solutions, verify them, and pick the best one, or let the agent explore more branches before committing. Things that would be too slow or too expensive with a standard autoregressive model become feasible.

There's also a nice property specific to diffusion. Because the model refines the whole output jointly, it's natural to do things like structured outputs, filling in the middle, or editing an existing piece of text or code rather than only appending to it. A lot of agent work is really editing: modifying a function, updating a plan, correcting a tool call. That fits the diffusion paradigm well.

And finally, voice and real-time agents, like customer support, are a big area. There you have a hard latency budget, and anything that brings response time down while keeping quality high directly improves the user experience. So anywhere you're running many calls in a loop, or a human is waiting on the other end, is where Mercury tends to shine.

r001.rationale: The response presents Mercury as useful for long-horizon coding agents that iterate; it does not judge Mercury a poor fit for unattended agentic tasks.

r002.rationale: It identifies voice and real-time agents as a strong use case, explaining that lower response latency improves the experience when a human is waiting.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key thing to understand about Mercury is that it's a diffusion-based language model, and the main thing that buys you is speed. We're generating tokens in parallel rather than one at a time, so you get something like five to ten times the throughput of a comparable autoregressive model at the same quality level. And when you think about where that matters most, it's really in agentic settings, because agents are fundamentally latency-bound in a way that a chat assistant isn't.

If you're chatting with a model, a few hundred milliseconds here or there, you barely notice. But an agent might be making dozens or hundreds of model calls to accomplish a single task. It's planning, it's calling a tool, it's reading the result, it's deciding what to do next, maybe it's backtracking. All of that latency compounds. So if each step is five times faster, the whole loop is five times faster, and that changes what's actually practical to build.

The place we've seen the most pull so far is coding. Things like code completion, code editing, where a developer is sitting there waiting. That's probably the most latency-sensitive application there is, because you're in the loop in real time. With Mercury Coder you can get a suggestion back before you've even finished thinking about what you wanted, and that's a qualitatively different experience than waiting a second or two.

But beyond coding, I think about things like voice agents, where you have a hard budget of a few hundred milliseconds before the conversation feels unnatural. And then more broadly, any kind of multi-step workflow where you'd like to do search, or sampling multiple candidates and picking the best one, or running a verifier. Those techniques are great, but they multiply your inference cost and latency, so people often can't afford them in production. If the base model is much faster and cheaper, suddenly you can explore more at test time, and that tends to make the agent more reliable too.

And there's one more thing that's specific to diffusion, which is that because the generation isn't strictly left to right, you have more flexibility in how you edit and refine. So for things like infilling, or revising an earlier part of the output based on something you figured out later, the architecture is a natural fit. We're still early in exploiting that, but I think that's where some of the most interesting agentic capabilities will come from longer term.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes that Mercury’s speed helps agentic workflows, but it does not judge Mercury a poor fit for unattended tasks that run for long periods.

r002.rationale: It identifies coding and voice agents as latency-sensitive, real-time settings where a person is waiting on the agent, and says faster responses change the experience.

astra-6.text:
I think the most compelling use cases are ones where the agent needs to take many sequential steps. It generates something, calls a tool, looks at the result, and then decides what to do next. In that setting, the latency of each generation really adds up, because you can’t start the next step until the previous one is finished.

So a coding agent is a good example: it might make a change, run a test, inspect an error, and try again. If you can make the generation faster, you can shorten that whole feedback loop. And you can also spend some of that time savings on additional attempts or checking the answer. That’s where I think Mercury could be especially useful—when faster generation translates into a more responsive agent or more work completed within the same time budget.

r001.rationale: It describes latency-sensitive, sequential agent work but does not judge Mercury to be a poor fit for tasks running unattended for long periods.

r002.rationale: It calls responsive agents a good use case, but does not identify fast interactions with a human in the loop.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most compelling use case is when you have a lot of sequential calls to a model. An agent might need to decide what to do, call a tool, look at the result, and then decide what to do next. The latency of each of those steps adds up, so making the model faster can have a big impact on how quickly the agent completes the task.

Coding is a good example, where you’re making a change, running a test, and using that feedback to try again. If you can shorten that loop, you can either get to an answer sooner or give the agent more opportunities to improve its solution within the same amount of time. That’s where I think Mercury can be particularly useful.

r001.rationale: The response describes latency-sensitive agent tasks but does not judge Mercury to be a poor fit for unattended, long-running tasks.

r002.rationale: It identifies fast sequential agent interactions as useful, but does not mention a human in the loop.
